title: Seeing many signs does not guarantee you keep the gift.
subtitle: Swapping a blessing for its opposite
then: Ibn Kathir lists what the Children of Israel witnessed with Moses: {reward}the parted sea, water from the rock, shade from the clouds, manna and quails{/reward}. Yet many {trap}changed Allah's favor{/trap} by preferring disbelief. The Prophet ﷺ is told to ask them how many signs they were given.
now: The recovery you prayed for. The job that came through. The baby who arrived safe. A year later it is just normal life, and the prayers have gone quiet. {idea}A favor can be exchanged slowly, by forgetting.{/idea}
old: I have seen Allah help me, so my faith is settled.
new: Every sign I was given is a trust, and I can still trade it away if I stop being grateful.
try: Write down one clear answer to a prayer from your past. Thank Allah for it today by name.

title: They laugh now. The final ranking is posted later.
subtitle: When this world is made to look like everything
then: Ibn Kathir describes people {trap}satisfied with this life, collecting wealth but not spending it{/trap} where Allah asked, and mocking believers who give. On the Day of Return the believers are {reward}above them{/reward}, and Allah gives without limit.
now: Your cousin jokes that you are naive for giving to the masjid appeal while he upgrades his car. Your colleagues smirk when you skip the after-work drinks. {idea}The laughter is real, but it is not the last word.{/idea}
old: If people mock my choices, maybe I am the one losing.
new: Mockery today says nothing about who stands higher on the Day.
try: Give something small today that nobody will see or praise.

title: People split not from lack of proof, but from rivalry.
subtitle: Why clear guidance still gets argued away
then: Ibn Abbas said there were ten generations between Adam and Nuh, {idea}all on the religion of truth{/idea}. Then they disputed, and Allah sent prophets. Those given the Book {trap}differed after clear proofs came, out of rivalry{/trap}. The Prophet ﷺ prayed at night: guide me to the truth in what they differed over.
now: The family argument that started over one comment and is now about who is right. The online debate where nobody is actually looking for the answer anymore. {trap}Winning has replaced finding.{/trap}
old: When I argue about religion, I am just defending the truth.
new: Sometimes my disagreement is ego, not evidence, and I need to ask Allah to show me the truth.
try: Before your next disagreement, pray the Prophet's ﷺ words: guide me to the truth by Your leave.

title: Even the shaken asked, when is help coming? It is near.
subtitle: The path to Paradise runs through tests
then: Khabbab asked the Prophet ﷺ why he did not pray for their relief. He reminded them how {trap}believers before them endured terrible torture{/trap} without leaving their faith, and said: {idea}you are a hasty people{/idea}. The Companions were later shaken at the battle of the Confederates.
now: Third month of unemployment. The scan results that keep getting delayed. You have prayed, and you whisper, when? {reward}Asking when is not weakness. Even the messengers asked it.{/reward} The reply is: it is near.
old: If I were a real believer, this would not be so hard.
new: Being shaken is part of the path, and Allah's help is closer than it feels.
try: Tell Allah honestly today how tired you are, then say: Your help is near.

title: Your giving starts with the people closest to you.
subtitle: Who comes first when you spend
then: They asked the Prophet ﷺ what to spend, and the answer turned to where: {idea}parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler{/idea}. A hadith in the tafsir lists {idea}your mother, father, sister, brother, then the closest and the next{/idea}. Whatever good you do, Allah knows it.
now: You donate to an appeal online, but you have not called your mother in two weeks, and your brother is quietly struggling with rent. {reward}The groceries you drop at your parents' door count.{/reward}
old: Real charity is giving to big causes far away.
new: Good starts with the people Allah put closest to me, and none of it goes unseen.
try: Do one practical thing for a parent or relative today: a bill, a meal, a lift.

title: You might hate what is good for you, and love what harms.
subtitle: Your feelings are not the full picture
then: This verse came to the early community in Madinah, facing enemies who attacked them. Ibn Kathir notes it was {trap}difficult and heavy on their hearts{/trap}. Then the verse widens: {idea}one might want something that is not good for him{/idea}. Allah knows how things turn out; you do not.
now: The job offer that fell through and broke your heart. The move you resisted that became the best thing for your family. The relationship you begged for that would have hurt you. {idea}You were never seeing the whole map.{/idea}
old: If I hate something this much, it must be bad for me.
new: My dislike is real, but Allah sees the ending and I only see today.
try: Think of one thing you hated at the time that turned out good. Thank Allah for it.

title: A wrong is wrong, but blocking people from Allah is worse.
subtitle: When critics measure only your mistake
then: Abdullah bin Jahsh led a small group to Nakhlah to gather news. On what was {trap}the last day of the sacred month of Rajab{/trap}, a man of Quraysh was killed. The Prophet ﷺ said: I did not command you to fight in the sacred month. Quraysh made it a scandal. The verse {idea}admits the wrong is great, then names a greater one{/idea}: turning people from Allah and driving them out.
now: Your mistake goes viral in the family group chat, posted by the person who has wronged you for years. {idea}You can own your error without accepting that it is the only thing on the scale.{/idea} Then look at your own record the same honest way.
old: Either I admit everything they say or I defend myself completely.
new: I can own my wrong fully and still see the bigger picture fairly.
try: Admit one mistake today plainly, with no but after it.

title: Those who believed, left home, and strove hope for mercy.
subtitle: Even the sincere live on hope, not certainty
then: After Nakhlah, Ibn Kathir reports that the men of the raid {trap}felt they were destroyed{/trap}, criticized by their own brothers. This verse came after: those who believed, emigrated and strove {reward}hope for the mercy of Allah{/reward}, and He is Forgiving, Merciful.
now: You moved cities for a better deen, gave up a well-paid role, kept praying through hard years. Then one bad call and you feel worthless. {reward}Your whole record is still there. Hope is still yours.{/reward}
old: One mistake cancels everything I tried to do for Allah.
new: Sincere effort keeps me in hope of His mercy, even after I slip.
try: Recall one sacrifice you made for Allah, and ask Him for mercy with confidence.

title: Some benefit, bigger harm. And give what you can spare.
subtitle: Weighing honestly instead of just counting gains
then: Umar kept praying: O Allah, give us a clear ruling on wine. Ibn Kathir explains this verse was {idea}the first step{/idea}, before later verses in An-Nisa and Al-Ma'idah. It admits {reward}some benefit{/reward} but says {trap}the harm is greater{/trap}. The same verse asks what to spend: what you can spare.
now: The betting app that paid out once. The scrolling that sometimes teaches you something. You defend it with that one good thing. {idea}The question is not whether there is any benefit, but which side of the scale is heavier.{/idea}
old: As long as something has some good in it, I can keep it.
new: I should weigh the whole cost, not hold on to the small gain.
try: Pick one habit and list its real costs and gains side by side on paper.

title: Care for orphans like brothers. Allah knows who means harm.
subtitle: Handling what belongs to the vulnerable
then: The verse links back: think about {idea}this world and the next{/idea}. Then it answers a question about orphans: {idea}improving their situation is best{/idea}, and if you share life with them, {reward}they are your brothers{/reward}. Allah knows who intends harm and who intends good.
now: You are managing your late uncle's money for his kids. Or you are the auntie raising a niece. You worry about getting it wrong. {idea}Treat them like your own, keep your intentions clean.{/idea} Allah sees the heart behind the spreadsheet.
old: Looking after someone else's child is a burden I just have to manage.
new: They are my brothers and sisters, and Allah knows the good I intend.
try: Check in on a child who has lost a parent, or give something to support one.
